result.summary: A speaker who stayed a year with Circe tells how Picus, king of Ausonia, spurned Circe's love because of his wife Canens. Circe turned him into a woodpecker and his companions into beasts, and Canens wandered grieving until she vanished into thin air by the Tiber.

scenes.title: Picus and Canens introduced
scenes.summary: Picus, handsome king of Ausonia, is wooed by many nymphs but loves only Canens, a singer of great power. He rides out to hunt boar.

scenes.title: Circe tries to win Picus
scenes.summary: Circe sees Picus, lures him from his guards with a phantom boar and darkened sky, and begs for his love. He refuses out of faithfulness to Canens, and she threatens him.
scenes.stakes: Picus risks Circe's vengeance if he stays faithful to Canens.

scenes.title: Picus and his men transformed
scenes.summary: Circe turns Picus into a woodpecker with his purple and gold colours. When his attendants attack, she summons dark powers and turns them into beasts.
scenes.stakes: Picus loses his human form; his attendants risk death and are transformed.

scenes.title: Canens vanishes into air
scenes.summary: Canens searches six days and nights, then laments by the Tiber and dissolves into air. The place is named Canens.
scenes.stakes: Canens loses her husband and, finally, her own life.

scenes.title: The teller's stay ends
scenes.summary: The narrator says he spent a year with Circe, was ordered to sail on, and was frightened by her warning, so he stayed on these shores.
scenes.stakes: Perils of a dangerous sea voyage.

alias_notes.explanation: Circe's father the Sun is called a Titan, so she is named as his daughter.

notable_quotes.reason: Circe's fierce, memorable declaration of what a slighted woman in love can do.

analysis.text: Faithful love is punished by thwarted desire and magic, and the tale explains a bird's origin through metamorphosis.
The story gives Latium's early kings and place names a mythic origin, tying Roman land to legend.

fun_facts.text: Picus was associated in Roman tradition with the woodpecker, a bird sacred to Mars.

language_notes.text: Ausonia is an old poetic name for Italy; Picus is a legendary early king of Latium, son of Saturn in Roman tradition.
The speaker points to a statue or image of Picus nearby, so 'as thou beholdest' refers to a physical likeness.
The Olympic games were held every fifth year at Elis; the sentence says Picus was under twenty, too young to have seen four of them.
The daughter of the Sun is Circe, the enchantress; the Circæan fields are named after her, around Mount Circeo on the Latin coast.
'Suppliant' means one who humbly begs a favour; the goddess reverses her usual rank by pleading.
'With impunity' means without punishment or harm.
Turning to West and East twice each is a ritual gesture: magic repeated in set numbers, with three as the traditional charm number.
Latian means of Latium, the region of Italy around Rome. Picus is a legendary early king there.
Erebus and Chaos are primeval realms of darkness in the underworld. Hecate is the goddess of witchcraft and night, invoked in magic.
Tartessian means of Tartessus, in southwestern Spain; the poet uses it for the far western ocean where the sun sets.
Tiber is the river of Rome, here a god-like witness. Canens ends her life on its banks.
Ancient belief held that the swan sang a beautiful song just before dying, hence 'swan song'.
Daughter of Titan means Circe, whose father was the Sun (Sol), a Titan's son in Ovid's usage.

context_notes.text: This long list of rivers and springs places the nymphs in the real landscape of Latium.
Janus was the Roman two-faced god of doorways and beginnings; here he is the father of Canens by the nymph Venilia.
Circe's father is the Sun, and magic that darkens the moon and gathers clouds over him shows her power over nature.
Picus becomes a woodpecker, an Italian bird sacred to Mars, which explains its purple and gold colouring in the tale.
This is an aetiological ending: the story explains how a place got its name, a common Ovidian pattern.

literary_notes.text: Canens's song moves rocks, stills rivers and holds birds in flight, showing the extraordinary power of music.
Love as a flame running through her marrow expresses sudden, consuming passion.
Picus follows the phantom 'unconsciously,' chasing a vain hope that is Circe's trap, leading him from safety.
The rising triplet 'slighted, in love, a woman' ends with Circe naming herself, giving a menacing sense of what follows.
Picus, who rejected Circe, now strikes oaks in rage; his anger is expressed in the very bird-habit that marks his new form.
Weeping stones, bloody grass and phantoms build a vivid supernatural horror, showing the scale of Circe's power.
Canens' faint mournful singing is compared to a dying swan, foreshadowing her own fading away.
Melting with grief turns sorrow into physical dissolution, making her vanishing into air a literal outcome of emotion.
